children.name: pinneapple_arena.arena
children.doc:
Arena — main orchestrator for multi-model physics benchmarks.

Usage
-----
    arena = Arena.from_yaml("benchmark.yaml")
    arena.run()

    # or
    from pinneapple_arena import ArenaConfig, Arena
    cfg = ArenaConfig.from_dict({...})
    Arena(cfg).run()

Feature summary
---------------
  • ALL pinneapple_neural models via ModelRegistry.build()
  • pinneapple_physics compiled losses (when physics_preset is set)
  • pinneapple_data datasets (via DatasetConfig)
  • pinneapple_analysis inverse problems (via InverseConfig.enabled=True)
  • pinneapple_analysis UQ (via UQConfig.enabled=True)

evaluate it, verify the result, record the evidence, and let the engine pick

functions.name: rank_by_accuracy
functions.sig: (train_results: list[TrainResult], eval_results: list[dict[str, Any]], field_names: list[str]) -> list[tuple[str, float]]
functions.doc:
Pure-accuracy ranking: (name, mean_rel_error) sorted ascending
(best first). This is Arena's default, unchanged ranking behaviour.

functions.name: physics_aware_rank
functions.sig: (train_results: list[TrainResult], eval_results: list[dict[str, Any]], field_names: list[str], n_std: float = 2.0, residual_threshold: float | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Additive, opt-in comparison view layered on top of the default
pure-accuracy ranking.

Keeps ``ranking`` identical to :func:`rank_by_accuracy` (accuracy is
still what orders the models) but also flags any PINN-family model
whose ``physics_residual`` is an outlier relative to the group —
i.e. a model that *looks* accurate at the evaluation points but is
violating the PDE it was trained against. Flags are additive
annotations, never a silent re-ordering: a model that ranks #1 on
accuracy and gets flagged still ranks #1.

Parameters
----------
n_std:
    A model is flagged if its ``physics_residual`` exceeds
    ``median + n_std * std`` of the group of models that report one.
    Ignored (outlier test skipped) if fewer than 2 models report a
    residual.
residual_threshold:
    Optional absolute cutoff. If set, any model whose residual exceeds
    this value is flagged in addition to (not instead of) the
    relative-outlier test above.

Returns
-------
dict with keys:
    ``ranking``               — same as :func:`rank_by_accuracy`
    ``physics_residuals``     — {name: residual} for models that have one
    ``flagged_high_residual`` — names flagged as outliers, in ranking order
    ``group_median``, ``group_std`` — stats used for the outlier test
                                       (``None`` if too few data points)

children.name: pinneapple_arena.autoresearch
children.doc:
Autoresearch mode: an automated experiment loop over a single training script.

Pattern from karpathy/autoresearch (MIT, ``ROADMAP.md`` §11): a fixed-time-budget training script,
one metric, and a proposer that edits the script between runs; changes that improve the metric are
kept, the others reverted, and every trial is logged. Here, adapted to physics AI:

- ``program.md`` holds the research instructions and the physics context for the proposer.
- ``train.py`` is the only file that changes. It must print ``METRIC <name>=<value>`` (lower is
  better, e.g. relative L2 against a closed form) and respect ``PINNEAPPLE_TIME_BUDGET`` seconds.
- Edits are limited to the ``# >>> TUNABLE`` ... ``# <<< TUNABLE`` block (``NAME = value`` lines),
  which keeps each proposal small, reviewable and safe to apply automatically.
- Proposers: :class:`RandomSearchProposer` (no LLM, reproducible) and :class:`LLMProposer`
  (any provider of ``pinneapple_llm``, or your own ``llm_call(prompt, system=...) -> str``).

Every trial goes to ``results.tsv``; the best script so far is kept as ``best_train.py``.

    from pinneapple_arena.autoresearch import AutoResearch, RandomSearchProposer, init_workdir
    init_workdir("runs/poisson")  # program.md + train.py (1D Poisson PINN, rel-L2 vs sin(pi x))
    AutoResearch("runs/poisson", RandomSearchProposer({"LR": [1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2], "WIDTH": [16, 32, 64]}),
                 budget_s=60).run(max_trials=20)

children.name: pinneapple_arena.bundle_bench
children.doc:
Equal-budget PINN vs FNO on an external dataset, with the verification gates attached to the result.

The task this harness poses is the one an imported benchmark is actually for: reproduce a field ``u(t, x)`` over
a trajectory, and be scored where the model was not trained -- the last ``1 - train_fraction`` of the time steps.
Two families see the same field, the same split, the same optimiser budget and the same seed, are scored with the
same metric (relative L2) and are gated by the same checks:

``fno``
    a 1-D Fourier neural operator over the spatial axis, with the normalised time as a constant input channel and
    a position grid (plus any static fields named in ``config.inputs``, e.g. a permeability): a spectral model of
    the same map.
``pinn``
    a coordinate network ``(t, x) -> u`` trained on the same grid points (a data-supervised PINN). Pass
    ``residual=`` with a callable ``residual(model, t, x, u, du_dt, du_dx, du_dxx) -> Tensor`` to add a PDE term
    and make it a physics-informed one: this library cannot turn the bundle's ``physics.governing`` prose into an
    equation, and the module says so rather than pretending the residual is there.

Both are the smallest honest version of their family (a reduced budget on a CPU), so the numbers here compare the
*families on this data*, not either family against its best published result -- and the report says so.

    >>> from pinneapple_arena.bundle_bench import BenchConfig, run_benchmark
    >>> report = run_benchmark(bundle, BenchConfig(field="density", epochs=200))
    >>> print(report.to_markdown())          # rel-L2 per model, the leader, and the gates that ran

functions.sig: (bundle: PhysicsDataBundle, config: BenchConfig | None = None, *, models: Sequence[str] = ('pinn', 'fno'), residual: Callable[..., Any] | None = None, equation: str = '', parameters: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, conserved: str | None = None, ledger = None) -> BenchReport
functions.doc:
Train every model on the same split, score them the same way, and gate the best prediction.

Two sets of gates come back with the ranking: the **data** gates over the winning prediction
(:mod:`pinneapple_data.schema.gates`) and the **model** gates from
:mod:`pinneapple_veriphysics.surrogate_gates` -- accuracy, conservation and the PDE residual when ``equation=``
names one this library discretises (``"advection"``, ``"burgers"``, ``"diffusion"``, ``"wave"``). A gate that
cannot be asked reads "not run".

With ``ledger`` (a ``pinneapple_veriphysics.ledger.EvidenceLedger``) each model's held-out score is sealed with
the bundle digest as its input hash, so the words "the FNO reached 3e-2" have a record behind them.

children.name: pinneapple_arena.bundle_uq
children.doc:
Uncertainty of a surrogate, and a design search over it: INT-010.

The uncertainty that matters for a surrogate is **epistemic**: it was trained on this much data and stops varying
where the data stops. Measuring it needs several models, not one number, so :func:`seed_ensemble` trains the same
architecture on the same data with different seeds and reports what the disagreement between them looks like --
mean and standard deviation of the held-out relative L2, and the pointwise spread of the predictions themselves,
which is what a confidence band on a field is made of.

The design half is the same models used the other way: :func:`design_optimize` searches a box for the input that
minimises an objective evaluated through the surrogate, reports the best design found and ranks the inputs by rank
correlation with the objective -- the sensitivity a designer actually asks for ("does the fin height or the
thickness matter here?").

Neither is a promise: the ensemble's spread is a measure of disagreement between three models, not a posterior, and
the search is over the box it is given, not over the physics. The docstrings say so, and the report says so.

    >>> from pinneapple_arena.bundle_uq import seed_ensemble, design_optimize
    >>> uq = seed_ensemble(bundle, BenchConfig(field="density", epochs=80), seeds=(0, 1, 2))
    >>> uq.summary()
    >>> best = design_optimize(lambda d: float((d["thickness"] - 0.004) ** 2), {"thickness": (0.001, 0.01)})

classes.name: EnsembleReport
classes.doc: What several seeds of the same model say about each other on the held-out part of a trajectory.

classes.name: DesignResult
classes.doc: The best design found, what it scored, and which inputs moved the objective.

functions.name: seed_ensemble
functions.sig: (bundle: Any, config: Any, *, model: str = 'fno', seeds: Iterable[int] = (0, 1, 2), keep_predictions: bool = True) -> EnsembleReport
functions.doc:
Train ``model`` once per seed on the same split and report how much the answers disagree.

The spread is measured on the held-out time steps and normalised by the standard deviation of the data there, so
it reads as "the models disagree by this fraction of the signal" -- comparable across fields and units.

functions.name: spearman
functions.doc: Rank correlation, the dependence measure that does not assume the objective is linear in the input.

functions.name: design_optimize
functions.sig: (objective: Callable[[Mapping[str, float]], float], bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]], *, n: int = 64, seed: int = 0, maximize: bool = False) -> DesignResult
functions.doc:
Sample ``n`` designs by Latin hypercube, evaluate ``objective`` and keep the best.

``objective`` is whatever the caller wants to minimise -- a surrogate's prediction, a closed-form estimate, a
cycle of the solver. A budget of 64 evaluations is a search, not an optimiser: it is honest about what a cheap
surrogate makes possible without a gradient, and the sensitivity it reports is a rank correlation over the
sample, which is why it is given with the number of evaluations that produced it.

children.name: pinneapple_arena.config
children.doc:
ArenaConfig — structured configuration for PINNeAPPle Arena benchmarks.

Supports loading from YAML, JSON, or direct Python construction.

Example YAML
------------
problem:
  name: kovasznay_ns
  physics_preset: ns_incompressible_2d_default   # optional: use pinneapple_physics preset
  params:
    re: 40.0
  grid_n: 40
  n_col: 2000
  n_bc: 500

models:
  - name: VanillaPINN
    type: vanilla_pinn
    network:
      hidden: [128, 128, 128, 128]
      activation: tanh
    training:
      epochs: 2000
      lr: 5.0e-4
      grad_clip: 1.0

  - name: FNO-2D
    type: fno2d
    network:
      width: 32
      modes: 12
      layers: 4
    training:
      epochs: 600
      lr: 1.0e-3

  - name: MeshGraphNet
    type: meshgraphnet
    network:
      hidden_dim: 128
      n_message_passing: 6
    training:
      epochs: 600
      lr: 1.0e-3

# Optional: load a pinneapple_data dataset instead of a built-in problem
# dataset:
#   dataset_id: navier_stokes_2d
#   input_fields: [x, y]
#   output_fields: [u, v, p]
#   n_train: 1000

# Optional: inverse problem mode
# inverse:
#   enabled: true
#   params: [re]
#   n_obs: 100
#   noise_std: 0.01
#   method: adam
#   n_iters: 2000
#   lambda_reg: 1.0e-3

# Optional: decision mode -- the decision engine picks which models to train
# decision:
#   enabled: true
#   budget: 2                 # at most 2 models are trained
#   thresholds: {rel_l2: 0.05, residual: 1.0e-3}
#   evidence_path: outputs/decision_evidence.json

# Optional: uncertainty quantification
# uq:
#   enabled: true
#   method: mc_dropout     # mc_dropout | ensemble | aleatoric | decompose
#   n_samples: 50
#   dropout_rate: 0.1

output:
  dir: outputs/
  prefix: benchmark
  save_figures: true
  dpi: 150
  dark_theme: true

Decision mode: the decision engine chooses which configured models to train.

Instead of training every model in ``models``, the Arena asks
``pinneapple_decision`` which one to run first, trains and evaluates it,
verifies the result (``thresholds`` on ``rel_l2`` = mean relative L2 over the
fields and, for PINN-family models, ``residual`` = final PDE residual), records
the evidence, and asks again, until a result passes or ``budget`` models ran.

children.name: pinneapple_arena.custom_builder
children.doc:
High-level API for defining custom physics problems.

The user provides:
  - equation name and description
  - coordinate names and bounds
  - field names (unknowns)
  - PDE as a string (e.g. ``"eps * u_xx - k * u + f"``)
  - boundary/initial conditions as simple dicts
  - optional analytical solution for metrics

Everything else (loss generation, data sampling, Arena pipeline) is automatic.

Derivative notation in PDE strings
-----------------------------------
``u_x``  → ∂u/∂x       ``u_xx`` → ∂²u/∂x²
``u_t``  → ∂u/∂t       ``v_xy`` → ∂²v/∂x∂y
``p_yy`` → ∂²p/∂y²     etc.

All coordinate names and param names are available in the expression.
Math functions available: ``sin``, ``cos``, ``exp``, ``sqrt``, ``tanh``, ``log``,
``abs``, ``pi``, ``e``.

Examples
--------
1-D reaction-diffusion::

    from pinneapple_arena import define_problem
    import numpy as np

    prob = define_problem(
        name="reaction_diffusion",
        description="eps·u'' − k·u = f  on [0,1],  u(0)=u(1)=0",
        coords={"x": (0.0, 1.0)},
        fields=["u"],
        pde="eps * u_xx - k * u + (eps * pi**2 + k) * sin(pi * x)",
        bcs=[
            {"type": "dirichlet", "at": "x_min", "field": "u", "value": 0.0},
            {"type": "dirichlet", "at": "x_max", "field": "u", "value": 0.0},
        ],
        params={"eps": 0.1, "k": 1.0},
        analytical=lambda x, eps=0.1, k=1.0: {"u": np.sin(np.pi * x)},
    )
    prob.solve(models=["VanillaPINN", "SIREN"], epochs=3000)

2-D Poisson::

    prob = define_problem(
        name="poisson_2d",
        coords={"x": (0.0, 1.0), "y": (0.0, 1.0)},
        fields=["u"],
        pde="u_xx + u_yy + 2 * pi**2 * sin(pi * x) * sin(pi * y)",
        bcs=[{"type": "dirichlet", "at": "boundary", "field": "u", "value": 0.0}],
        params={},
        analytical=lambda x, y: {"u": np.sin(np.pi * x) * np.sin(np.pi * y)},
    )
    prob.solve(epochs=4000, output_dir="outputs/poisson/")

1-D+time heat equation::

    prob = define_problem(
        name="heat_1d_custom",
        coords={"x": (0.0, 1.0), "t": (0.0, 1.0)},
        fields=["u"],
        pde="u_t - alpha * u_xx",
        bcs=[
            {"type": "dirichlet", "at": "x_min", "field": "u", "value": 0.0},
            {"type": "dirichlet", "at": "x_max", "field": "u", "value": 0.0},
            {"type": "initial",   "at": "t_min", "field": "u",
             "value": lambda x, **kw: np.sin(np.pi * x)},
        ],
        params={"alpha": 0.1},
    )
    prob.solve()

functions.name: define_problem
functions.sig: (name: str, coords: dict[str, tuple[float, float]], fields: list[str], pde: str, bcs: list[dict[str, Any]], params: dict[str, float] | None = None, description: str = '', analytical: Callable | None = None, bc_weight: float = 10.0) -> EasyArenaProblem
functions.doc:
Define a custom physics problem with a declarative, high-level API.

All heavy lifting — loss compilation, training data generation, Arena
pipeline construction — is handled automatically.

Parameters
----------
name        : unique problem identifier (used in output filenames).
coords      : ordered mapping of coordinate name → (min, max) bounds.

              Examples::

                  {"x": (0.0, 1.0)}                     # 1D spatial
                  {"x": (0.0, 1.0), "y": (0.0, 1.0)}   # 2D spatial
                  {"x": (-1.0, 1.0), "t": (0.0, 1.0)}  # 1D + time
                  {"x": (0,1), "y": (0,1), "z": (0,1)} # 3D

fields      : list of unknown field names (e.g. ``["u"]``, ``["u", "v", "p"]``).

pde         : PDE as a string expression **equal to zero** (residual form).

              Derivative notation::

                  u_x   → ∂u/∂x        u_xx  → ∂²u/∂x²
                  u_t   → ∂u/∂t        v_xy  → ∂²v/∂x∂y

              Math available: ``sin``, ``cos``, ``exp``, ``sqrt``,
              ``tanh``, ``log``, ``abs``, ``pi``, ``e``.

              All coord names and param names are in scope.

bcs         : list of boundary/initial condition dicts::

                  {
                      "type" : "dirichlet",   # ignored by solver, kept for docs
                      "at"   : "x_min",       # location specifier (see below)
                      "field": "u",           # which field
                      "value": 0.0,           # float | str-expr | callable
                  }

              ``at`` options:

              * ``"x_min"`` / ``"x_max"`` / ``"y_min"`` / … — axis-aligned boundary
              * ``"t_min"`` — initial condition (alias for ``"t_min"``)
              * ``"boundary"`` — all exterior faces
              * ``"x=0.5"`` — arbitrary fixed value of a coord

              ``value`` can be:

              * a **float** — constant
              * a **string** expression using coord names and params
              * a **callable** ``f(**coords, **params) → array``

params      : dict of named scalar parameters available in the PDE string.
description : human-readable description (shown in plots).
analytical  : callable ``f(**coord_arrays, **params) → dict[field_name, array]``
              providing the exact solution. Used for L2/Linf metrics and as
              supervised interior targets.
bc_weight   : multiplier on the BC loss term (default 10).

Returns
-------
EasyArenaProblem
    A fully configured problem with a ``.solve()`` convenience method.

Quick example
-------------
::

    import numpy as np
    from pinneapple_arena import define_problem

    prob = define_problem(
        name="my_poisson",
        coords={"x": (0.0, 1.0), "y": (0.0, 1.0)},
        fields=["u"],
        pde="u_xx + u_yy + 2 * pi**2 * sin(pi * x) * sin(pi * y)",
        bcs=[{"type": "dirichlet", "at": "boundary", "field": "u", "value": 0.0}],
        params={},
        analytical=lambda x, y: {"u": np.sin(np.pi * x) * np.sin(np.pi * y)},
    )
    prob.solve(models=["VanillaPINN", "SIREN"], epochs=4000,
               output_dir="outputs/my_poisson/")

children.name: pinneapple_arena.dataset_bench
children.doc:
dataset_bench.py -- High-level benchmark API using pinneapple_data datasets.

Every dataset registered in ``pinneapple_data`` has a recommended preset here
(input/output fields, model list, training config, mode).  The public surface
is intentionally minimal:

  * :data:`DATASET_PRESETS`        -- full preset table, keyed by dataset_id
  * :func:`benchmark_dataset`      -- one-liner: load preset, build Arena, run
  * :func:`list_benchmarks`        -- show available presets (with category filter)
  * :func:`get_benchmark_preset`   -- retrieve a preset dict for inspection

Usage
-----
::

    from pinneapple_arena.dataset_bench import benchmark_dataset

    # Simplest usage -- all defaults from preset
    benchmark_dataset("burgers_1d", output_dir="outputs/burgers/")

    # Override epochs and model list
    benchmark_dataset(
        "kovasznay_ns",
        models=["VanillaPINN", "SIREN"],
        epochs=3000,
        mode="pinn_data",
        output_dir="outputs/kovasznay/",
    )

    # Regression dataset
    benchmark_dataset("airfoil_noise", output_dir="outputs/airfoil/")

    # List everything available
    from pinneapple_arena.dataset_bench import list_benchmarks
    list_benchmarks()
    list_benchmarks(category="pde")

children.name: pinneapple_arena.dataset_problems
children.doc:
DatasetProblem — ArenaProblem backed by a real pinneapple_data dataset.

Converts any dataset registered in ``pinneapple_data`` into a first-class
Arena problem, handling:

  * **PDE datasets** (burgers_1d, heat_1d, kovasznay_ns …)
    Structured spatial/temporal grids are properly flattened into
    ``(N, in_dim)`` training arrays without losing coordinate alignment.

  * **Timeseries datasets** (lorenz63, spring_mass, van_der_pol …)
    Direct time→state regression, or sliding-window sequences.

  * **Regression datasets** (airfoil_noise, concrete_strength …)
    Standard feature-matrix → target, no spatial structure assumed.

  * **Geometry datasets** (naca0012, cylinder_2d …)
    Interior/boundary point arrays surfaced as collocation data.

  * **Physics-hybrid mode**  (``mode="pinn_data"``)
    Combines a supervised data loss (from the dataset) with an autograd
    physics residual for any dataset that maps to a known PDE type.

Usage
-----
::

    from pinneapple_arena.dataset_problems import DatasetProblem

    prob = DatasetProblem.from_dataset(
        "burgers_1d",
        input_fields=["x", "t"],
        output_fields=["u"],
        mode="supervised",       # or "pinn_data" for PINN hybrid
        Nx=256, Nt=101,          # kwargs forwarded to load_dataset()
    )
    # prob is a fully registered ArenaProblem — use it in any Arena config
    Arena(ArenaConfig.from_dict({
        "problem": {"name": prob.name},
        "models": [...],
    })).run()

children.name: pinneapple_arena.decision_mode
children.doc:
Arena as a decision laboratory: the decision engine picks which models to train.

Default Arena mode trains every configured model and ranks them. Decision mode
(``Arena.run_decision(budget=...)`` or ``decision: {enabled: true}`` in the
config) instead runs the ``pinneapple_decision`` loop over the configured
models::

    DECIDE   which configured model to train next  (PhysicsChoice "arena_model";
             options = model names; constraints: geometry support, budget,
             not already trained in this session)
    EXECUTE  Arena._train_one + Arena._evaluate_one  (ArenaExecutor)
    VALIDATE ThresholdVerifier on rel_l2 (mean relative L2 over fields) and, for
             PINN-family models, residual (final PDE residual); any Verifier works
    LEARN    EvidenceStore; the next decision reads the verification tags and
             penalizes the family of a model that failed

and stops when a result passes verification (``stop_when_passed``) or after
``budget`` trained models. Models that were never chosen are not trained.

The engine decides *which experiment to run*; the metrics come from the Arena's
own training and evaluation against the problem's reference data. A metric the
Arena did not produce (e.g. ``residual`` for a supervised model) is a check that
did not run, not a pass.

Fine-tuning / retraining runners — one per pip-installable model in the
catalog (light or heavy; manual-install-only repos have nothing to run
in-app regardless, same as for inference).

Three different things happen under one "fine-tune" action in the UI,
distinguished by `ModelResult.metrics["mode"]`:

  - "finetune"    — a real, short (CPU, seconds) gradient-based training or
                    variational-optimization loop on the model's own
                    learnable parameters.
  - "reconfigure" — the model has no learnable weights (it's a physics
                    solver/engine, not a trained network) or the weights
                    require a real dataset+checkpoint this demo can't
                    provide, so "retraining" means re-running the same
                    solver with user-supplied parameters instead, or (for
                    checkpoint-only frameworks) re-confirming a real import
                    with an honest note about what a full fine-tune needs.
                    Either way it's a genuine run, just not gradient descent
                    on a loss.

Every model without a pip package (git-only repos, non-Python tools) has no
entry here — `run_finetune()` falls back to the same manual-install status
inference already reports for them, since nothing changes about whether the
app can execute their code.

children.doc:
External model catalog: references to third-party physics-ML libraries and the glue that runs them.

Every entry (`ModelSpec`) is a reference: name, organisation, repository URL, licence (with where it was read),
citation and install instructions. No third-party code is copied here: each runner in
``pinneapple_arena.external.runners`` imports the real library at run time, builds a minimal instance, runs one
forward pass or simulation on a small synthetic input (``demo_datasets``) and reports a ``ModelResult`` whose
``status`` says what really happened:

========================== ===============================================================================
``ok``                     the library was imported and a real call ran; the output is genuine
``not_installed``          pip-installable, not installed here (the result carries the pip command)
``skipped_heavy``          GPU / heavy dependency, run only with ``include_heavy=True``
``manual_install``         no pip package (git-only, Julia, C++); the result carries the clone/build steps
``failed``                 it ran and raised; the exception is in ``error``
``finetune_not_supported`` no fine-tune / reconfigure routine for this library
========================== ===============================================================================

A result is never invented. Datasets (The Well) have their own catalog (``DATASETS``) and a ``probe`` action that
loads one real sample through the dataset's own loader.

    from pinneapple_arena import external as ext

    ext.MODELS_BY_SLUG["deepxde"].license            # 'LGPL-2.1' (read from the repository's LICENSE file)
    r = ext.call_infer("deepxde")                     # ModelResult; status 'not_installed' without deepxde
    ext.run_benchmark(ext.select_slugs(category="pinn"))

Command line: ``python -m pinneapple_arena.external --list`` / ``--model deepxde --action infer``.

Two aggregations are kept apart, because mixing them changes the numbers (see the note in the vehicle-aerodynamics
benchmark):
- **per geometry, then averaged**: relative L2 of a geometry (``||y_hat - y|| / ||y||`` over all of its points), and
  the mean over the test geometries;
- **pooled over all points**: R^2 and the absolute errors, computed on the points of all geometries at once.

Every reported number carries a bootstrap confidence interval when it can, and a comparison between two models is
reported with the paired bootstrap (mean difference, its interval, the share of geometries where one wins) plus the
sign-flip permutation and Wilcoxon signed-rank p-values over the per-geometry scores.

Nothing here is vehicle-specific: pass in ``(N, C)`` arrays per geometry and get the same protocol the papers use.

    from pinneapple_arena.fieldbench.metrics import mean_relative_l2, pooled_r2, paired_bootstrap, leaderboard

classes.name: ModelScore
classes.doc: One row of a leaderboard: the per-geometry scores, the summary and the cost.

classes.name: PatchwiseProtocol
classes.doc:
Evaluate a prediction given on a *subset* of points against the full reference field.

The vehicle-aerodynamics benchmark compares three ways of getting a field on the full mesh out of a model that
only predicts where it is asked (subsampled evaluation, interpolation to the rest, and a patchwise pass):

- ``subsampled``: score only the points the model saw;
- ``interpolated``: interpolate the predicted subset onto all points (nearest or RBF) and score the whole field;
- ``patchwise``: predict on overlapping patches of points and keep the central part of each, so no interpolation
  is involved.

methods.name: score
methods.sig: (points_all: np.ndarray, values_all: np.ndarray, points_sub: np.ndarray, values_sub_pred: np.ndarray) -> dict
methods.doc: (prediction on all points, reference on all points) for the chosen mode.

functions.name: relative_l2_per_geometry
functions.doc:
Relative L2 of every geometry: ``||pred - true||_2 / ||true||_2`` over its points and channels.

The shapes have to agree, not only the number of values: a one-component prediction flattened against a
three-component field has a third of the entries, and an equal *count* (a wider mesh, say) would let that pass and
score two different things against each other.

functions.name: mean_relative_l2
functions.doc: The benchmark's headline error: relative L2 averaged over the geometries (not over the points).

functions.name: pooled_r2
functions.doc: R^2 over every point of every geometry at once (``1 - SS_res / SS_tot``).

functions.name: absolute_errors
functions.doc: Absolute error of every point of every geometry, pooled.

functions.name: error_percentiles
functions.doc: The error profile: median *relative* error per point, and the P50/P90/P95/P99 of the absolute error.

functions.name: extreme_of_field
functions.sig: (field, channel: int = 0, mode: str = 'min', frames: str = 'all') -> float
functions.doc:
The extreme of one channel over the points (and the frames) of a single field — the KPI a crash report quotes.

``mode="min"`` is how a crash result reads the displacement along the impact direction (the structure travels
*into* the obstacle, so the peak is the most negative value); ``mode="max"`` is the same for a magnitude or a
pressure. ``frames="all"`` takes the extreme over every stored frame, ``"last"`` only the final one, and an int
picks that frame. An empty or all-padded field returns ``nan`` instead of a silent zero.

functions.name: extreme_errors
functions.sig: (preds, truths, *, channel: int = 0, mode: str = 'min', frames: str = 'all', n_boot: int = 2000) -> dict
functions.doc:
Score a surrogate on the extremes of the fields — the quantity-level KPI, next to the field-level metrics.

A field surrogate can be compared to the reference twice, and the papers report the first while the engineer asks
the second: the mean relative L2 over the whole field (``mean_relative_l2``), and the relative error of the one
number the design was run for (peak displacement, peak force). They are computed from the same predictions and
are not substitutes — a model can shade every point by 5 % and still get the peak wrong, or the other way round.

Returns the per-geometry reference and prediction, their absolute and relative errors, and the mean/median/max
relative error with a bootstrap interval on the mean.

functions.name: bootstrap_ci
functions.sig: (values, n_boot: int = 2000, alpha: float = 0.05, strata = None, rng = None) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc:
Percentile bootstrap of the mean, ``[lo, hi]`` at ``1 - alpha``.

``strata`` (one label per value) resamples inside each stratum and rescales the counts to the stratum's share, so
a benchmark whose categories are unequal gets an interval that is not dominated by the largest one.

functions.name: paired_bootstrap
functions.sig: (a, b, n_boot: int = 10000, rng = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Paired comparison of two per-geometry score vectors (lower is better).

Returns the mean difference ``a - b`` with its bootstrap interval, the share of geometries where ``a`` wins, and
the two-sided sign-flip permutation and Wilcoxon signed-rank p-values.

functions.name: model_cost
functions.sig: (model, sample_input, device: str = 'cpu', n_warm: int = 2, n_rep: int = 10) -> dict
functions.doc:
Parameters, latency per geometry, throughput and peak memory of a forward pass.

``sample_input`` is a dict of tensors (the model's keyword arguments, batch of one geometry). The latency is the
median of ``n_rep`` timed forwards after ``n_warm`` warm-ups, without gradient.

functions.name: score_model
functions.sig: (name: str, family: str, preds, truths, *, cost: dict | None = None, notes: str = '', n_boot: int = 2000, strata = None, rng = None) -> ModelScore
functions.doc: Score one model with the protocol above (per-geometry relative L2 with a bootstrap interval, pooled R^2).

functions.name: leaderboard
functions.sig: (rows: list[ModelScore], *, order_by: str = 'rel_l2', digits: int = 4) -> str
functions.doc: Markdown table of the scores, the interval of each, and the cost columns when they are present.

children.summary: Metrics of a field surrogate benchmarked over many geometries — the conventions the two vehicle benchmarks use.

children.name: pinneapple_arena.fieldbench.models
children.doc:
Model rows of a field-surrogate benchmark, built through one interface so that one trainer trains them all.

Every entry is a builder of an ``nn.Module`` whose forward is ``(x, *, part, part_id, thickness, time, mask) ->
(B, N, C)`` for a steady field or ``(B, T, N, C)`` for a transient one — the interface the trainer and the metrics
expect. The adapters below bring the library's own operators (``Transolver``, ``TransolverLite``) and the point
models into it without renaming anything.

Two things this module deliberately does not do: it never labels a stand-in with the name of a published model it is
not (an approximation carries its own name, and its note says what it approximates), and it never silently drops a
row — a model that cannot be built is reported as unavailable, with the reason.

classes.name: OperatorSetAdapter
classes.sig: (operator: nn.Module, out_dim: int = 1, in_dim: int | None = None, time_dim: int = 8, t_max: float = 1.0)
classes.doc:
Wrap a point operator (``(B, N, in_dim) -> (B, N, out_dim)``) into the set-to-set interface.

The operator sees the coordinates plus any extra per-node channels, and — when the benchmark is transient — a
Fourier encoding of the requested time, frame by frame. This is the honest way to put a steady operator on a
transient benchmark: same weights for every frame, time as an input, no invented temporal head.

methods.name: forward
methods.sig: (x: torch.Tensor, *, part = None, part_id = None, thickness = None, extra = None, time = None, mask = None, **_) -> torch.Tensor

functions.name: build_model_specs
functions.sig: (*, in_dim: int = 3, out_dim: int = 1, transient: bool = False, n_frames: int = 8, n_parts: int = 8, scale: str = 'small', extra_dim: int = 0) -> list[dict]
functions.doc:
The model rows of a benchmark, one spec per architecture (``{"name", "family", "build", "notes"}``).

``scale="small"`` keeps every model trainable on a laptop-sized corpus; ``scale="paper"`` uses the widths the
vehicle-aerodynamics benchmark reports (a TransolverLarge of ~7.6 M parameters, a wide residual point model), which
needs a GPU to be worth the wall time. ``transient`` rows add a temporal head (the hierarchical model) or the time
as an input channel (the operators and the point models).

functions.name: available_models
functions.doc: Names the specs report as buildable on this machine (a constructor is attempted with tiny sizes).

children.summary: Model rows of a field-surrogate benchmark, built through one interface so that one trainer trains them all.

children.name: pinneapple_arena.fieldbench.protocol
children.doc:
Containers and the run of a field-surrogate benchmark over many geometries.

A benchmark here is a list of *samples*, one per geometry: the points the model may look at (and is asked to predict
on), the field values at those points, and whatever per-point extra channels the model can use (part labels, wall
thickness) plus, for a transient field, the times of the frames. Splits are named lists of sample ids — the official
split of the corpus, or a category split that holds a whole category out (the zero-shot experiment).

    from pinneapple_arena.fieldbench import FieldSample, FieldDataset, run_benchmark

classes.name: FieldSample
classes.doc:
One geometry of a field benchmark.

``points`` (N, 3); ``values`` (N, C) for a steady field or (T, N, C) for a transient one; ``parts`` (N,) semantic
part labels when the structure has them; ``part_ids`` (N,) dense ids; ``thickness`` (N,) a wall thickness or any
per-node scalar; ``extra`` (N, D) the remaining per-node channels a surrogate may read — a design vector broadcast
to every node is the case this exists for, and it is what makes a benchmark *parametric*: without it a model can
only interpolate between the geometries it was trained on, never answer for a design it has not seen; ``times``
(T,) the frame times of a transient field. ``meta`` is for the record, never for the model.

methods.name: inputs
methods.sig: (*, with_parts: bool = True, with_extra: bool = True) -> dict
methods.doc: The keyword arguments a surrogate's ``forward`` takes for this sample (batch of one).

methods.name: target
methods.doc: The field to learn, shaped as the model outputs it: (N, C) or (T, N, C).

classes.name: FieldDataset
classes.doc: A named set of samples plus the splits a benchmark scores on.

methods.name: hold_out_category
methods.sig: (category: str, val_fraction: float = 0.2, seed: int = 0) -> FieldDataset
methods.doc: Everything else trains, a held-out category is the test set (the zero-shot protocol).

methods.name: save
methods.doc: One ``.npz`` per dataset: a JSON header plus the arrays (points, values and the optional channels).

functions.name: normalize_geometry
functions.doc:
Map the coordinates of every sample by the *same* transform (the mean centre of the corpus and the largest
extent), so the geometry stays comparable between samples and the network sees O(1) numbers. The values are left
untouched — the metrics are reported in physical units.

functions.name: subsample_nodes
functions.sig: (dataset: FieldDataset, max_nodes: int, seed: int = 0) -> FieldDataset
functions.doc:
Keep at most ``max_nodes`` nodes per sample, at random but reproducibly, with their part labels and frames.

A field benchmark on a 3,000-node crash mesh trains a transformer on 3,000 tokens per frame; retaining a node
subset is what the published crash benchmark does as well ("the same retained node subset" for every row), so the
models are compared on a subset while the dataset keeps every node for anyone who wants the full field.

functions.name: run_benchmark
functions.sig: (specs, dataset: FieldDataset, *, epochs: int = 30, batch_size: int = 2, lr: float = 0.001, device: str | None = None, patience: int = 10, seed: int = 0, standardize: bool = True, verbose: bool = False, n_boot: int = 2000) -> dict
functions.doc:
Train and score every model spec on the dataset's splits; returns scores, predictions and the leaderboard.

A spec is ``{"name", "family", "build": callable -> nn.Module, "uses_parts": bool, "uses_extra": bool,
"notes": str}``; a row that does not read the extra channels is built without them and the trainer leaves them
out of the batch, so a geometry-only row can be scored on a dataset that carries the design vector. Nothing about
the architecture lives here: the caller builds the model (from the registry, or its own class), so a benchmark row
is never a stand-in for another architecture.

functions.name: write_report
functions.doc: Write the leaderboard and the per-geometry detail as markdown plus a JSON sidecar.

children.summary: Containers and the run of a field-surrogate benchmark over many geometries.

children.name: pinneapple_arena.fieldbench.tabular
children.doc:
The tabular half of a component-scale campaign: a design vector in, a handful of scalar quantities out.

The crash corpus of a pole impact comes with a tabular benchmark (seven design variables -> peak wall force,
deceleration, internal energy, plastic work, kinetic-energy absorption), and the interesting question there is not
which net is fashionable but whether a gradient-boosted tree beats a linear model by enough to justify it. This
module runs that comparison once, with the same split and the same fixed hyperparameters for every family (a
zero-tuning protocol: no model gets a search the others did not), and reports R^2, MAE, RMSE and MAPE per target plus
the mean, with the feature sensitivity of the tree models.

Every model is optional: scikit-learn is required, XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost are used when installed, and a model
that is not installed is reported as unavailable with the reason instead of being quietly dropped from the table.

    from pinneapple_arena.fieldbench.tabular import load_table, benchmark_tabular, write_table_report
    table = load_table("runs/pole_impact/pole_impact_quantities.csv", inputs=DESIGN_KEYS, targets=TARGET_KEYS)
    result = benchmark_tabular(table, seed=42)
    print(result["table"])

functions.name: available_regressors
functions.doc: Which model families this machine can build (scikit-learn always, the boosters when installed).

functions.name: probe_family
functions.sig: (factory, x, y, timeout_s: float = 120.0) -> str | None
functions.doc:
Fit one family on a handful of rows **in a child process**; return the reason it is unusable, or ``None``.

A model whose wheels crash the interpreter (a segmentation fault in a booster compiled against another NumPy, say)
cannot be caught by ``try/except`` in this process, and a benchmark that dies halfway tells nobody which row was
at fault. The probe runs the smallest possible fit in a fork, so a crash becomes a reported row.

functions.name: load_table
functions.sig: (csv_path: str, *, inputs: list[str], targets: list[str], filter_ok: bool = True) -> dict
functions.doc:
Read a campaign's quantities table into ``{"x", "y", "targets", "inputs", "rows"}``.

Rows marked ``out_of_envelope`` (a run that left the strain envelope of the solver) are dropped when
``filter_ok`` is set, and the count of dropped rows is reported — never silently.

functions.name: benchmark_tabular
functions.sig: (table: dict, *, seed: int = 42, test_fraction: float = 0.15, val_fraction: float = 0.15, standardize_targets: bool = False) -> dict
functions.doc:
Fit every available family on the same split and score it per target, with the mean over targets.

The split is frozen by ``seed`` (70/15/15 as the reference campaign does) and the same rows are used for every
model, so the comparison is paired.

functions.name: feature_sensitivity
functions.doc:
Permutation importance of every design variable, averaged over the tree models and the targets that exist.

Returned as ``{target: {input: relative importance}}`` with the importances of each target normalised to one.

functions.name: write_table_report
functions.sig: (result: dict, path: str, sensitivity: dict | None = None) -> str
functions.doc: Write the tabular leaderboard (markdown) and the same numbers as JSON.

children.name: pinneapple_arena.fieldbench.trainer
children.doc:
Training and inference of a set-to-set field surrogate: one geometry in, the field on its own points out.

The library trains pointwise fields (``pinneapple_arena.pointwise.training``) and grid operators, but a surrogate over
*many geometries* needs a different batching: every sample is a geometry with its own point count, and the batch is
padded to the largest one, with a mask that keeps the padding out of the pooling and the loss. That is what this
trainer does, plus the bookkeeping a benchmark row needs (target standardisation from the training split only,
early stopping on the validation split, best-weights restore, gradient clipping, and the cost of a forward pass).

    from pinneapple_arena.fieldbench.trainer import train_field_model, predict_field_model
    hist = train_field_model(model, dataset, train_ids, val_ids, epochs=30, device="cpu")
    preds = predict_field_model(model, dataset, dataset.splits["test"], device=hist["device"])

Nothing here is tuned per architecture: the same loop trains every model row of a benchmark, which is the point of a
benchmark (a different budget per model makes the comparison meaningless). When a model needs a different budget the
caller records it in the row's notes.

functions.name: collate_samples
functions.sig: (dataset, ids, *, standardize: dict | None = None, uses_parts: bool = True, uses_extra: bool = True) -> dict
functions.doc:
Pad a list of samples into one batch.

Returns a dict with ``x`` (B, N, 3), ``mask`` (B, N), the optional ``part``/``part_id``/``thickness``/``extra``
/``time`` channels, ``y`` (B, N, C) or (B, T, N, C) standardised when ``standardize`` is given, ``channels``, and
the point count of every sample (to slice the padded prediction back). ``extra`` is the sample's own per-node
channels — the design vector of a parametric benchmark, broadcast to its nodes — padded with zeros like the rest,
and left out entirely when ``uses_extra`` is false (the geometry-only ablation reads the same dataset).

functions.name: train_field_model
functions.sig: (model, dataset, *, train_ids, val_ids, epochs: int = 30, batch_size: int = 2, lr: float = 0.001, weight_decay: float = 1e-05, device: str | None = None, patience: int = 10, seed: int = 0, standardize: bool = True, grad_clip: float = 1.0, uses_parts: bool = True, uses_extra: bool = True, verbose: bool = False) -> dict
functions.doc: Train one surrogate on the training split, early-stop on the validation split, restore the best weights.

functions.name: predict_field_model
functions.sig: (model, dataset, ids, *, device: str = 'cpu', uses_parts: bool = True, uses_extra: bool = True, batch_size: int = 2) -> list[np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Predict every sample of ``ids``; returns one array per sample with the field's own shape (physical units).

children.doc:
Benchmark of field surrogates over many geometries (surface pressure over a car body, displacement over a crash
structure): containers, metrics with bootstrap intervals, the paired significance tests, one trainer for every row,
and the leaderboard.

    from pinneapple_arena.fieldbench import (FieldSample, FieldDataset, normalize_geometry, subsample_nodes,
                                             run_benchmark, build_model_specs, write_report)

children.name: pinneapple_arena.model_factory
children.doc:
Build any Arena-supported model from a ModelConfig.

Uses ModelRegistry.build() (+ instantiate normalization) from pinneapple_neural
to access ALL registered models (~80+). Falls back to hardcoded builders for the
most common types when the registry is unavailable.

All 80+ model keys registered in ModelRegistry are supported:
  vanilla_pinn, inverse_pinn, siren, modified_mlp, pielm, pinnsformer, vpinn,
  xpinn, xtfc, fno, fno2d, deeponet, pino, gno, uno, meshgraphnet, gnn,
  equivariant_gnn, graphcast, neural_ode, latent_ode, neural_cde, hnn,
  transformer, informer, tft, lstm, gru, conv1d, conv2d, esn, koopman,
  pod, dmd, sindy, vae, dense_ae, ... and all Noether variants

functions.name: build_model
functions.sig: (cfg: ModelConfig, in_dim: int = 2, out_dim: int = 1, edge_in_dim: int = 0) -> nn.Module
functions.doc:
Instantiate any pinneapple model from a ModelConfig.

Uses ModelRegistry + instantiate() for automatic kwarg normalization
and filtering. Supports all 80+ registered models.

Parameters
----------
cfg          : ModelConfig — type key + NetworkConfig
in_dim       : physical/node feature input dimension
out_dim      : number of output fields
edge_in_dim  : edge attribute dimension (graph models only)

children.name: pinneapple_arena.nas
children.doc:
Architecture + hyperparameter search over the existing model catalog.

**What this is**: a *search-based* joint selection of (architecture family,
architecture hyperparameters, learning rate) over a fixed, already-registered
catalog (``pinneapple_neural.architectures.ModelRegistry``), driven by the
same Optuna TPE-sampler-with-median-pruner / random-search-fallback
machinery that ``pinneapple_neural.trainer.adaptive_sweep`` already uses.
Each Optuna "trial" both picks an architecture *and* samples that
architecture's hyperparameters (architecture choice is treated as just
another categorical hyperparameter — a flat search space, exactly the shape
``AdaptiveSweepConfig.param_space`` already expects), builds it via
``ModelRegistry.build()``, trains it for a small number of epochs on a real
``ArenaProblem`` via the real ``pinneapple_arena.trainer.train_pinn`` path,
and scores it from the real evaluation metrics (+ optionally the real
``TrainResult.physics_residual``).

**What this is not**: this is *not* a differentiable / weight-sharing NAS
(no DARTS-style supernet, no shared weights across candidates, no gradient
w.r.t. architecture choice). Every trial trains an independent model from
scratch. That is a deliberate scope decision — a true weight-sharing NAS
would be a much larger undertaking than the existing infrastructure (a
fixed architecture catalog + a black-box Optuna sweep) naturally supports,
and "search over the catalog + its hyperparameters" is what is actually
useful on top of what already exists (:mod:`pinneapple_arena.arena`'s
Arena, :mod:`pinneapple_neural.trainer.adaptive_sweep`'s AdaptiveSweep).

Why only re-implement part of ``adaptive_sweep``'s Optuna wiring
------------------------------------------------------------------
``adaptive_sweep.run_adaptive_sweep`` samples one *flat, unconditional*
parameter space every trial and returns a plain list of trial dicts — no
access to the underlying ``optuna.Study`` object. That flat-space model is
exactly what we want here too (architecture name + every candidate
architecture's hyperparameters, all sampled every trial; the trial function
below simply ignores whichever candidates' hyperparameters weren't the ones
selected for that trial — wasted samples, but harmless with the small
trial budgets a search inner-loop like this uses). But ``NASResult`` is
required to expose the raw ``optuna.Study`` (useful for external
introspection, e.g. ``optuna.visualization``), which
``run_adaptive_sweep``'s return type cannot carry. Since touching
``adaptive_sweep.py`` is out of scope for this module, :func:`search_architecture`
reuses ``adaptive_sweep``'s actual parameter-sampling primitives
(``_suggest_optuna``/``_suggest_random`` — the part that knows how to turn a
``("float"|"int"|"categorical", args)`` spec into a sampled value, including
log-uniform ranges) and follows the exact same
``TPESampler`` + ``MedianPruner`` / "``ImportError`` -> dependency-free
random-search fallback" pattern, rather than writing a second, parallel
parsing of the parameter-spec mini-language.

classes.name: ArchitectureCandidate
classes.doc:
One searchable architecture: its ``ModelRegistry`` key, its own
hyperparameter search space (in the same ``ParamSpec`` mini-language
``AdaptiveSweepConfig.param_space`` uses — ``("float"|"int", (lo, hi))``,
optionally ``(..., "log")``, or ``("categorical", (choices,))``), and a
function that turns one sampled-hyperparameter dict into the exact
kwargs ``ModelRegistry.build(name, **kwargs)`` needs. The build-kwargs
indirection exists because constructors are not uniform — e.g.
``modified_mlp`` wants an actual ``Type[nn.Module]`` for ``activation``
where ``vanilla_pinn`` wants a plain string; ``instantiate()`` filters
*unknown* kwargs but does not type-convert known ones, so this mapping
has to be exact per architecture rather than generic.
fields: build_kwargs_fn: Callable[[dict[str, Any], int, int], dict[str, Any]]

classes.name: ArchitectureSearchSpace
classes.doc:
Which architectures are candidates, plus each one's hyperparameter
search space and a shared learning-rate range applied to every
candidate (learning rate isn't architecture-specific, so it lives
outside `candidates` rather than being duplicated in each one).

functions.name: search_architecture
functions.sig: (problem: ArenaProblem, search_space: ArchitectureSearchSpace | None = None, n_trials: int = 20, physics_aware: bool = False, lam: float = 1.0, epochs_per_trial: int = 300, n_train: int = 64, n_bc: int = 32, n_col: int = 128, grid_n: int = 12, device: str = 'cpu', seed: int | None = None, timeout: float | None = None, **train_kwargs) -> NASResult
functions.doc:
Search over ``search_space`` (architecture name + each architecture's
hyperparameters, jointly) for the model that best solves ``problem``.

Each trial: samples an architecture name and that architecture's
hyperparameters (+ a shared learning rate) from ``search_space``,
builds it via ``ModelRegistry.build``, trains it for
``epochs_per_trial`` epochs via the real ``train_pinn`` path (small
epoch budget by design — this is a search *inner loop*, not a full
training run; raise ``epochs_per_trial`` for a more accurate search at
the cost of wall-clock time), evaluates it on ``problem``'s held-out
grid via the real ``evaluate_model``, and scores it via :func:`_score`.

Uses Optuna's TPE sampler + median pruner when Optuna is installed
(same as ``pinneapple_neural.trainer.adaptive_sweep``), else falls back
to dependency-free random search — no pruning in that case, matching
``adaptive_sweep``'s own fallback behaviour.

Parameters
----------
problem : an ``ArenaProblem`` (e.g. from ``pinneapple_arena.problems.get_problem``).
    Must support ``supervised_data`` + ``pinn_residuals`` (all built-in
    Arena problems do) since every default candidate architecture
    trains through ``train_pinn``.
search_space : candidate architectures + their hyperparameter ranges.
    Defaults to :data:`DEFAULT_CANDIDATES` (``vanilla_pinn``,
    ``modified_mlp``, ``siren``) wrapped in an ``ArchitectureSearchSpace``.
n_trials : number of architecture+hyperparameter combinations to try.
physics_aware : if True, penalize accuracy by the trained model's
    ``TrainResult.physics_residual`` (see :func:`_score`).
lam : the accuracy/physics-residual tradeoff weight, only used when
    ``physics_aware=True``.
epochs_per_trial, n_train, n_bc, n_col, grid_n : kept small by default
    (this is a search mechanism, not a full training run) — override
    for a more faithful (slower) search.
timeout : optional wall-clock budget in seconds for the whole search
    (Optuna backend: passed straight to ``study.optimize(timeout=...)``;
    random-search fallback: checked between trials).
**train_kwargs : forwarded to ``TrainingConfig`` for every trial (e.g.
    ``grad_clip``, ``scheduler``, ``optimizer``, ``weight_decay``) —
    unrecognized keys are silently dropped, ``epochs``/``lr`` are
    ignored here since they are controlled by ``epochs_per_trial`` and
    the per-trial sampled learning rate respectively.

Returns
-------
NASResult

children.name: pinneapple_arena.pointwise
pinneapple_arena.pointwise.adapters
children.doc:
Input adapters between the arena's pointwise data and PINNeAPPle architectures.

Every arena problem is pointwise field regression: a batch of coordinates
X of shape (N, in_dim) maps to field values of shape (N, out_dim), and the
physics loss differentiates u(x_i) with respect to x_i by autograd. Many
PINNeAPPle architectures, however, take grids or sequences — channels-first
(B, C, L) for FNO / conv1d, (B, C, H, W) for conv2d, (B, H, W, C) for AFNO,
(B, T, D) for transformers, RNNs, TCNs and reservoirs. Handed a flat (N, d)
tensor they either crash or silently treat the N points as one sample.

The adapters below treat every point as its own sample of spatial / temporal
extent 1. That keeps each prediction a function of its own point only (no
mixing across points, independent of point order), which is exactly what the
autograd physics residual requires.

Three groups:
- PointwiseAdapter  — gradient-trained models; reshape in, flatten out.
- ClosedFormAdapter — models whose readout is solved in closed form via
  fit(X, y) (ELM, hybrid RBF, ESN readouts); trained by the pipeline's
  closed-form path instead of gradient descent.
- NOT_APPLICABLE    — unsupervised trajectory / snapshot models (Koopman/EDMD,
  POD, DMD, HAVOK, ARIMA). Their fit() takes a time series or snapshot matrix
  and no target, so a coordinates→field regression cannot train them.

PDE-residual losses of the arena problems, ``(model, {"X": collocation points}) -> (loss, info)``.

Loss lookup order for each problem:
  1. Native PyTorch autograd residual of this module, built with the experiment's parameters (nu, alpha, c, ...)
  2. The PINNeAPPle preset's compiled PDE residual (``pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compile_problem``) via the
     explicit preset_key, then via problem_id; it uses the preset's own parameters, and only its ``pde`` term is
     used (boundary and initial conditions come in through the data). The preset's coordinate order must match
     the arena data (e.g. ``(x, t)`` for Burgers).
  3. None  (supervised-only training)

The source arena tried the preset first, but called it with an outdated signature, so every preset loss raised
and was skipped silently; the wrapper below adapts it, and the native residual (parameter-aware) comes first.

3. Native PyTorch autograd implementation from ``_NATIVE_LOSS_FACTORIES``
4. ``None``  — experiment continues with supervised loss only

children.name: pinneapple_arena.pointwise.training
children.doc:
Training and scoring of one architecture on a pointwise field problem (the PINNeAPPle Arena protocol).

Every arena problem is a field regression: coordinates ``(N, in_dim)`` in, field values ``(N, out_dim)`` out. A
model is built from the PINNeAPPle registry (``pp.build_model``) and, when it takes grids or sequences, wrapped by
``pinneapple_arena.pointwise.adapters``. It is trained on reference samples with an optional PDE residual on
separate collocation points (``pinneapple_arena.pointwise.losses``), early-stopped on a validation split, and
scored on a held-out test split (``field_metrics``, ``prediction_quality``).

No stand-in is ever trained under an architecture's name: when the registry cannot build an architecture for this
data, ``instantiate_model`` raises ``ArchitectureUnavailable`` (or ``ArchitectureNotApplicable``) and the caller
reports the architecture as failed, with the reason.

    from pinneapple_arena.pointwise import training as T
    in_dim, out_dim = T.problem_dims("burgers_1d")
    model = T.instantiate_model("vanilla_pinn", in_dim, out_dim)
    out = T.train_torch_model(model, X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val, X_col, loss_fn, n_epochs=200, lr=1e-3, device="cpu")
    metrics = T.field_metrics(T.predict(model, X_test), y_test)

children.doc:
Pointwise field benchmarks: the problems, reference data, losses, model adapters and training protocol of the
PINNeAPPle Arena app (``apps/pinn_arena``).

An arena problem is a field regression on coordinates: ``(N, in_dim)`` points in, ``(N, out_dim)`` field values
out. For each of the 34 catalog problems (``PROBLEMS_CATALOG``) a reference dataset comes from an analytic or
numerical solution (``DatasetGenerator``), the PDE residual from a PINNeAPPle preset or a native autograd residual
(``PhysicsLossGenerator``), and any registry architecture (``ARCHITECTURES_CATALOG``) is built through
``pp.build_model`` and, if it expects grids or sequences, wrapped so each point is its own sample (``adapters``).
``training`` trains one architecture under the arena protocol (data loss + warmed-up, magnitude-balanced PDE
residual on separate collocation points, cosine LR, early stopping on a validation split, best weights restored)
and scores it on a held-out split; ``leaderboard.aggregate`` ranks architectures over many experiments.

    from pinneapple_arena import pointwise as pw

    gen = pw.DatasetGenerator("burgers_1d", {})
    ref = gen.generate(n_samples=2000)                     # coords (N, 2) = (x, t), solution (N, 1)
    loss_fn = pw.PhysicsLossGenerator("burgers_1d", {}).compile_losses()
    model = pw.instantiate_model("vanilla_pinn", 2, 1)     # ArchitectureUnavailable if the registry can not build it

This differs from ``pinneapple_arena.Arena`` (YAML-driven runs of ``ArenaProblem`` PINN benchmarks with their own
residuals) and from ``pinneapple_arena.regimes`` (equal-budget surrogate rankings per data regime): the problems
here carry UI metadata (equations, parameters, column hints for uploads) and the protocol is the one the app runs.

  Elliptic                poisson_2d, laplace_2d, biharmonic_2d, helmholtz_2d
  Transport               advection_diffusion_1d
  Waves                   wave_1d, klein_gordon_1d, nls_1d
  Nonlinear / Solitons    burgers_1d, kdv_1d
  Reaction-Diffusion      allen_cahn, fisher_kpp_1d, fitzhugh_nagumo_1d

classes.doc: 2D Stokes (Poiseuille) flow: u = 1-y², v = 0, p = -2x.

classes.name: Heat1D
classes.doc: 1D heat: u_t = alpha*u_xx,  u = exp(-alpha*pi^2*t)*sin(pi*x).

classes.name: Heat2D
classes.doc: 2D heat: u_t = alpha*(u_xx+u_yy).

classes.name: ConvectionDiffusion1D
classes.doc:
Steady 1D convection-diffusion: c*u_x = eps*u_xx.
Analytical: u = (exp(c*x/eps) - 1)/(exp(c/eps) - 1) on [0,1], u(0)=0, u(1)=1.

classes.name: DarcyFlow2D
classes.doc: 2D Darcy: -Δp = f,  p = sin(πx)sin(πy),  f = 2π²sin(πx)sin(πy).

classes.name: Laplace2D
classes.doc: 2D Laplace: Δu = 0,  u = sin(πx)sinh(πy)/sinh(π).

classes.name: Poisson2D
classes.doc: 2D Poisson: Δu = -2π²sin(πx)sin(πy),  u = sin(πx)sin(πy).

classes.name: Helmholtz2D
classes.doc: 2D Helmholtz: u_xx + u_yy + k²u = f,  u = sin(πx)sin(πy).

classes.name: Biharmonic2D
classes.doc: 2D Biharmonic (thin plate): Δ²u = f, u = sin(πx)sin(πy), f = 4π⁴*u.

classes.name: AdvectionDiffusion1D
classes.doc:
1D advection-diffusion: u_t + c*u_x = nu*u_xx.
Analytical: u = exp(-nu*pi²*t)*sin(pi*(x - c*t)).

classes.name: Wave1D
classes.doc: 1D wave: u_tt = c²u_xx,  u = sin(πx)cos(πct).

classes.name: KleinGordon1D
classes.doc:
1D Klein-Gordon: u_tt - u_xx + m²u = 0.
Analytical: u = cos(kx)cos(ωt),  ω² = k² + m².

classes.name: NLS1D
classes.doc:
1D NLS bright soliton: |ψ(x,t)| = A*sech(A*(x-vt)).
We solve for (u, v) = (Re ψ, Im ψ) using the real/imaginary split.
Solves i*psi_t + psi_xx + 2*|psi|^2*psi = 0 (nonlinearity coefficient 2).

classes.name: Burgers1D
classes.doc:
1D Burgers: u_t + u*u_x = nu*u_xx, u(x,0) = -sin(pi*x), u(-1,t)=u(1,t)=0.

Exact solution via the Cole-Hopf transform u = -2*nu*phi_x/phi, where
phi solves the heat equation with phi(x,0) = exp(-integral(u0)/(2*nu)).
The convolution integral against the heat kernel is evaluated with
Gauss-Hermite quadrature (this closed form has no elementary expression
for a sinusoidal initial condition, unlike the previous placeholder).

classes.name: KdV1D
classes.doc:
1D KdV: u_t + 6u*u_x + u_xxx = 0.
Soliton: u = -2c*sech²(sqrt(c)*(x - 4c*t)).

classes.name: AllenCahn
classes.doc: 1D Allen-Cahn: u_t = eps²u_xx + u - u³.  Tanh interface.

classes.name: FisherKPP1D
classes.doc:
1D Fisher-KPP: u_t = D*u_xx + r*u*(1-u).
Exact Ablowitz-Zeidler traveling wave: u = [1/(1+exp(w*(x-v*t)))]^2
with v = 5*sqrt(D*r/6) and w = sqrt(r/(6D)).

classes.name: FitzHughNagumo1D
classes.doc:
1D FitzHugh-Nagumo excitable media (two fields: v, w).
v_t = v_xx + v(1-v)(v-a) - w + I,  w_t = eps*(v - gamma*w).

classes.doc:
2D plane-strain linear elasticity (manufactured solution).
Displacement: u = sin(πx)sin(πy), v = 0.
Body force computed from Lamé equations.

classes.name: BlackScholes1D

1D Black-Scholes PDE for a European call option.
V_t + r*S*V_S + sigma^2*S^2/2*V_SS - r*V = 0.
Analytical via BS formula (evaluated on (log-price, time) grid).

children.name: pinneapple_arena.regimes
children.doc:
Regime arena: which method works best for a physical problem, per data regime, under one protocol.

``run_regime_arena(data, ...)`` trains every candidate of ``pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.methods`` that applies to
the data, with

* **equal data**: one split (fixed seed) shared by every method and every model seed;
* **equal compute**: the same ``ComputeBudget`` for every iterative method (``train_within_budget``), one-shot fits
  report the time they used;
* **the same stopping rule**: budget spent, best of ten validation checkpoints (iterative methods);
* **several seeds**: the model seed varies, the data does not; every number has its spread across seeds;

and measures, on data no method trained on, per regime:

==================  =============================================================================================
interpolation       random held-out samples inside the training distribution
few_data            the same held-out samples, training on ``few_data_fraction`` of the training samples
extrapolation       the distribution-shift set: one end of an input, or the edge of the input space
geometry_change     whole groups (geometries, cases) held out, when the data has groups
steep_fronts        fields: the held-out samples with the steepest gradients (top quartile of max |grad u|): a
                    proxy for discontinuities
==================  =============================================================================================

plus training time, inference time per query, model size, and physics violations: the share of predictions that
break the dataset's declared constraints (``pinneapple_data.audit.constraint_mask``) and, for fields with a declared
PDE, the finite-difference residual of the predictions relative to that of the reference data. The data splits are
audited independently by ``pinneapple_data.audit.audit_dataset`` (the PC451-PC453 checks of ``pinneapple check``:
finite values, duplicates, train/test leakage, declared constraints). Numerical-solver baselines (a callable
``solve(X, coords)``) are timed and scored on the same held-out samples.

Nothing is estimated: a regime that cannot be built from the data is reported as unavailable with the reason.

children.name: pinneapple_arena.serving_bench
children.doc:
Serving benchmarks: what a trained surrogate costs per call, in PyTorch and as an ONNX graph. INT-013.

A surrogate that is accurate and slow is not a product. The number that decides whether a model can sit behind an
API is latency at a realistic batch size and how it scales with it, so this module measures:

* **PyTorch** on CPU (and CUDA when it is there), after a warm-up, reporting p50 / p95 milliseconds and throughput;
* **ONNX** through ``onnxruntime``, when the package is installed, on the same inputs -- and the agreement between
  the two outputs, because a silently different ONNX graph is a serving bug that a latency table alone would hide;
* the **export** itself, when ``onnx`` can be written, by whichever of PyTorch's two exporters can lower the model.

Every missing piece is reported as a note in the result rather than crashing: a machine without ``onnxruntime`` still
gets the PyTorch numbers and a line saying what is not measured. The benchmark is CPU-first and single-stream, which
is the shape of the API this platform serves; a throughput number from a batched GPU run would answer a different
question.

**Three export attempts, in this order.** The TorchScript exporter (``dynamo=False``) is tried first: it is quick and
it covers the pointwise architectures most of this platform's surrogates have. When it refuses an operator, the graph
exporter (``dynamo=True``, opset 18, needs ``onnxscript``) is tried, because the two do not support the same set. When
both refuse -- which is what a spectral model does, since the FNO's convolution keeps **complex tensors** and neither
exporter lowers them (the graph exporter reports ``No decompositions registered for the complex-valued input``) -- the
model is rewritten in real arithmetic by
:func:`pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators.fno_export.to_exportable` and exported like any other module.
That rewrite is a dense cosine/sine transform instead of an FFT, so the graph it produces is not the graph PyTorch
runs; ``max_abs_difference`` is what says whether the substitution was faithful, and it is reported for exactly that
reason. Which attempt produced the graph is in ``ServingReport.exporter``: "it exported" and "which exporter" are
different facts about a serving stack.

    >>> from pinneapple_arena.serving_bench import benchmark_model
    >>> report = benchmark_model(model, example_input, path="surrogate.onnx")
    >>> print(report.to_markdown())

children.name: pinneapple_arena.showcase
children.doc:
Four contrasting PINN architectures trained on the same viscous Burgers problem, ranked by accuracy and by
Arena's physics-aware view.

Problem: ``burgers_1d`` (u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx, u(x, 0) = -sin(pi x) on [-1, 1], nu = 0.01/pi; Raissi, Perdikaris &
Karniadakis 2019, J. Comput. Phys. 378), reference by the Cole-Hopf solution inside the problem class. A steep front
forms near x = 0 around t ~ 0.3 and persists to t = 1.

The run uses Arena's own pieces (:func:`~pinneapple_arena.model_factory.build_model`,
:func:`~pinneapple_arena.trainer.train_pinn`, :func:`~pinneapple_arena.trainer.evaluate_model`,
:func:`~pinneapple_arena.arena.rank_by_accuracy`, :func:`~pinneapple_arena.arena.physics_aware_rank`), one model at
a time so a caller can report progress. ``physics_aware_rank`` never reorders the accuracy ranking; it flags models
whose PDE residual is an outlier of the group (median + n_std * std) and, when ``residual_threshold`` is given,
above that absolute value too. The relative test alone can miss models that are all bad together: with four
models, a model with a residual far above the others raises the group std with it (see the app README for a
measured case).

Per-architecture budgets (``DEFAULT_ARCHITECTURES``) were tuned in the source project for convergence on the front:
Vanilla PINN 4x64 for 12,000 epochs, SIREN 3x64 with omega_0 = 15 for 4,000, PIELM (frozen random hidden layer,
trained output layer) 128 features for 5,000, XTFC (constrained basis, trained output layer) for 400. A full run
takes minutes on a CPU; tests use a few epochs per model.

Architectures left out on purpose: ``vpinn`` builds the same network as ``vanilla_pinn`` and its weak-form loss is
not used by ``train_pinn``, so it would run as a copy of Vanilla PINN; ``hash_grid_mlp`` and ``bench_fourier_mlp``
collapsed towards the trivial u = 0 (low residual, ~90 % error) in the source project's tuning runs.

doc:
pinneapple_arena — YAML/JSON-driven multi-model physics benchmark runner.

Features
--------
  * ALL pinneapple_neural models via ModelRegistry.build() (~80+ architectures)
  * pinneapple_physics compiled losses (when physics_preset is set)
  * pinneapple_data datasets (DatasetConfig)
  * pinneapple_analysis inverse problems (InverseConfig.enabled=True)
  * pinneapple_analysis UQ (UQConfig.enabled=True)

Quick start
-----------
    from pinneapple_arena import Arena

    arena = Arena.from_yaml("my_benchmark.yaml")
    arena.run()

    # programmatic:
    from pinneapple_arena import ArenaConfig
    cfg = ArenaConfig.from_dict({
        "problem": {"name": "kovasznay_ns", "params": {"re": 40.0}},
        "models": [
            {"name": "VanillaPINN", "type": "vanilla_pinn",
             "network": {"hidden": [128, 128, 128, 128]},
             "training": {"epochs": 2000, "lr": 5e-4}},
            {"name": "FNO-2D", "type": "fno2d",
             "training": {"epochs": 600, "lr": 1e-3}},
            {"name": "MeshGraphNet", "type": "meshgraphnet",
             "training": {"epochs": 600, "lr": 1e-3}},
        ],
        "output": {"dir": "outputs/", "prefix": "benchmark"},
    })
    Arena(cfg).run()

Dataset mode
------------
    cfg = ArenaConfig.from_dict({
        "problem": {"name": "kovasznay_ns", "params": {}},
        "dataset": {
            "dataset_id": "navier_stokes_2d",
            "input_fields": ["x", "y"],
            "output_fields": ["u", "v"],
            "n_train": 2000,
        },
        "models": [...],
    })

With UQ
-------
    cfg = ArenaConfig.from_dict({
        ...,
        "uq": {"enabled": True, "method": "mc_dropout", "n_samples": 50},
    })

Decision mode (the decision engine picks which models to train)
---------------------------------------------------------------
    report = Arena(cfg).run_decision(budget=2)   # at most 2 models trained
    # or in the config: "decision": {"enabled": True, "budget": 2}
    # see pinneapple_arena/decision_mode.py and pinneapple_decision/README.md

With inverse problem
--------------------
    cfg = ArenaConfig.from_dict({
        ...,
        "inverse": {"enabled": True, "params": ["re"], "n_iters": 1000},
    })
